blocks: The fourth mode, C D E F♯ G A B♭ on C, approximates harmonics 8 through 14 of a fundamental on C. Writers on call it the acoustic or overtone scale for that reason.
The collection is one note away from both the major scale (lowered third) and Dorian (raised seventh).
Also called Aeolian and pure minor. On C: C D E♭ F G A♭ B♭. Steps in semitones: 2 1 2 2 1 2 2. The sixth mode of Music/Scale/Major.
named the mode on A Aeolian in the Dodecachordon ( ). Before that, a D-final piece with a B♭ sounded the same collection while still counting as Dorian.

Common-practice minor was never this collection alone. Cadences raised the seventh, first through musica ficta and later in notation, and melodic lines raised or lowered the sixth as voice leading required. Natural, Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic and Music/Scale/Minor/Melodic are later pedagogical slices of one flexible minor mode.
Aeolian folk song keeps the minor dominant (v) and cadences without a leading tone.
Rock and film music use the Aeolian progressions i–♭VII–♭VI and i–♭VI–♭VII, which treat ♭VII as a dominant substitute. In C: Cm–B♭–A♭.
In jazz the Aeolian chord-scale fits a minor chord functioning as vi in a major key, where Dorian would put the raised sixth against the key.

The scale shares its key signature with its relative major. Baroque composers sometimes wrote minor pieces with one flat fewer than the modern signature, a holdover from Dorian notation; see Music/Scale/Dorian.
The ♭6 separates Aeolian from Dorian. Many melodies described as "minor" use only scale degrees 1 through 5 and never decide between them.

The MicroFreak's "Minor" setting is listed in its manual as C D E♭ F G A B♭ B, which lacks A♭, the note that separates natural minor from Dorian, and adds B natural. See Microfreak/UG/15 Using Scales/01 Scale Settings and Music/Scale/Dorian/Bebop. The Launchpad's "Natural Minor" setting carries this scale's name; its manual lists no pitches.
Also called the tetrardus authentic mode or Mode 7. On C: C D E F G A B♭. Steps in semitones: 2 2 1 2 2 1 2. The fifth mode of Music/Scale/Major.
The ancient Greek Mixolydian octave species ran from B to B, the collection now called Locrian. The medieval G mode inherited the name in the Carolingian renaming; see Music/Scale/Dorian.
In polyphony the G mode's seventh was routinely raised to F♯ at cadences, so much "Mixolydian" Renaissance music cadences as if in G major.

Folk traditions that end tunes without a leading tone favor it. Irish and Scottish dance tunes are often Mixolydian, and the Great Highland bagpipe chanter plays a Mixolydian scale on A with a flat seventh.
Rock uses its ♭VII as a third functional chord beside IV and V. The progression I–♭VII–IV–I closes "Hey Jude", and the Beatles' "Norwegian Wood" is Mixolydian throughout.
In jazz chord-scale theory it is the default scale over an unaltered dominant seventh chord.
The tonic triad is major, the triad on 5 is minor (G B♭ D on C), and the subtonic chord ♭VII is major. Cadences come from ♭VII–I or IV–I instead of V–I.
Inverting its step pattern gives Music/Scale/Minor/Natural.
Also called the pentatonic, gong mode in Chinese theory, and the MicroFreak's "Pentatonic" setting. On C: C D E G A. Steps in semitones: 2 2 3 2 3.

Five-note scales without semitones appear in traditions with no historical contact: Chinese, Korean, Japanese, West African, Andean, Scottish and Appalachian music among them. Chinese theory derived its five tones, gong shang jue zhi yu, from a chain of fifths by the third century BCE.

European art music took it up as a marker of the exotic or the rural. heard the Javanese gamelan at the Exposition Universelle in Paris, and "Pagodes" (Estampes, ) is built on pentatonic collections. Javanese slendro tuning divides the octave into five near-equal steps, so the Western pentatonic is only an approximation of what he heard.
Folk melodies such as "Auld Lang Syne" and "Amazing Grace" are pentatonic.
Music education uses it for improvisation because it contains no semitones and no tritone. The Orff Schulwerk and methods start children on it.
Country, gospel and rock guitar use the major pentatonic for major-key soloing. Its five modes include Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Minor.
It is a stack of four perfect fifths (C G D A E).
The pitch-class complement of Music/Scale/Major is a pentatonic collection: the black keys of a piano form G♭ major pentatonic.
Also called la-pentatonic in solmization and yu mode in Chinese theory. On C: C E♭ F G B♭. Steps in semitones: 3 2 2 3 2. The fifth mode of Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Major.

and Kodály's fieldwork after found that the oldest layer of Hungarian peasant song is in a minor pentatonic, often with a melody that repeats a fifth lower in its second half. Bartók set out that finding in The Hungarian Folk Song ( ). It overturned the assumption that Hungarian music meant the style hongrois of Music/Scale/Minor/Hungarian.
The scale is also the foundation of blues and rock melody, where Music/Scale/Blues adds a ♭5 to it.
Rock and blues guitar organize improvisation around five fingerboard patterns of this scale, the "boxes".
Over a dominant seventh chord, the ♭3 grates against the chord's major third. Blues players treat that clash as the idiom.
Kodály pedagogy uses la-pentatonic for early minor-mode songs.
Every note of the scale is a chord tone or tension of a minor eleventh chord on the tonic (C E♭ G B♭ F), so the scale can be played over that chord with no avoid notes.
Also called the deuterus authentic mode or Mode 3. On C: C D♭ E♭ F G A♭ B♭. Steps in semitones: 1 2 2 2 1 2 2. The third mode of Music/Scale/Major.
The ancient Greek Phrygian octave species ran from D to D, the collection now called Dorian. The medieval name shifted with the rest of the Greek names; see Music/Scale/Dorian.

In chant and polyphony the E mode was hard to cadence in, because no leading tone rises to the final. Renaissance cadences in the E mode pair F–E in the bass with D–E above it. Heard from A minor, the result sounds like a half cadence.

That cadence outlived the mode. The Baroque "Phrygian half cadence", iv6–V in minor, uses the same half-step bass descent to the dominant. The two-chord Adagio of 's Brandenburg Concerto No. 3 is one.
Flamenco's characteristic sound is usually Phrygian with a major tonic, close to the fifth mode of Music/Scale/Minor/Harmonic, over the Andalusian cadence i–♭VII–♭VI–V.
Heavy metal leans on the ♭2 for darkness, often as a riff that alternates the tonic with ♭II.
In jazz chord-scale theory it fits a minor seventh chord functioning as iii, and the sus4♭9 chord voiced over it.
Carnatic music's Hanumatodi, melakarta 8, is this collection. See Music/Scale/Todi for the different Hindustani Todi.
It is the inversion of the major scale: the major step pattern read downward from the tonic gives Phrygian.
Phrygian and Locrian are the only diatonic modes with a ♭2. The ♭II triad sits a half step above a minor tonic, the relation the Neapolitan chord borrows in common-practice minor.
The tonic has no dominant: the triad on 5 is diminished (G B♭ D♭).
In sargam: S r g M' P d N. On C: C D♭ E♭ F♯ G A♭ B. Steps in semitones: 1 2 3 1 1 3 1.
One of 's ten Hindustani thaats, named for raga Todi. See Music/Scale/Marwa for how a thaat relates to the ragas inside it.
The principal raga is Miyan ki Todi. Its name ties it to Miyan Tansen, the singer at Akbar's court in the .
The Carnatic equivalent parent scale is Shubhapantuvarali, melakarta 45.
Miyan ki Todi is a late-morning raga. Pa is weak or skipped in ascent, and the lowered Re, Ga and Dha are sung slightly flat of their equal-tempered pitches, with slow oscillation.
Gujari Todi drops Pa entirely; Bilaskhani Todi takes its notes from the Bhairavi thaat yet keeps the Todi name.
The name points to two different scales. Carnatic Todi, Hanumatodi or melakarta 8, has the notes of Music/Scale/Phrygian, while Hindustani Todi has a raised fourth and a raised seventh.
Its step pattern, 1 2 3 1 1 3 1, contains two augmented seconds, like Music/Scale/Minor/Hungarian, from which it differs only in the second degree.
Also 's first mode of limited transposition. On C: C D E F♯ G♯ A♯. Steps in semitones: 2 2 2 2 2 2.
Glinka used a descending whole-tone scale for the sorcerer Chernomor in Ruslan and Lyudmila ( ), and Russian composers after him kept it for the supernatural.
made it a harmonic field. "Voiles" (Préludes, Book I, – ) stays on one whole-tone collection for most of its length and turns pentatonic in the middle.
Messiaen listed it first among his modes of limited transposition in Technique de mon langage musical ( ), and said he avoided it because Debussy and Dukas had used it so thoroughly.
Impressionist harmony, and later film and television, use it for dreams, flashbacks and suspended time.
Jazz uses it over a dominant seventh chord with a ♯5 and 9 (C7♯5, C9♯5), and made descending whole-tone runs a signature.

There are only two distinct whole-tone collections, the even and the odd pitch classes. Every rotation of the scale is the same scale, so it has no modes. On a device with root selection, the twelve roots produce only two sets of pitches.
It contains no perfect fifth, no leading tone and no minor or major triad; every triad built from it is augmented. No note can function as a tonic without help from outside the scale.
The French augmented sixth chord (A♭ C D F♯ in C) is a four-note subset of the scale, a pivot between functional and whole-tone harmony.
